title: Data transformation
summary: Use dplyr and the pipe to explore a year of bike trips. Keep and sort rows, change columns, count groups, and see when an average can mislead.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes dplyr

steps.explain: `library(tidyverse)` attaches dplyr, whose verbs this lesson uses, along with readr and the rest of the core tidyverse.

steps.title: A year of trips: read_csv()

runs.task: Read `data/trips.csv` into a variable called `trips` with `read_csv()`.

steps.explain: `trips` has {n_trips} rows, one for every trip in 2025. Each verb in this lesson takes a data frame and returns a new one, which the Console prints. `trips` itself stays as it is unless you assign the result with `<-`.

steps.title: Keep rows: filter() and the pipe

runs.purpose: keep the trips casual riders made on e-bikes
runs.task: Keep the trips where `member_type` is "casual" and `bike_type` is "electric", with `filter()`. Type the pipe, `|>`, with Ctrl+Shift+M.

runs.purpose: keep the trips that started or ended at station 101
runs.task: Keep the trips that started or ended at station 101: `start_station` or `end_station` is 101.

steps.explain:
The pipe, `|>`, hands what's on its left to the function on its right as its first argument: `trips |> filter(…)` means `filter(trips, …)`. Ctrl+Shift+M types it. `filter()` keeps the rows where the conditions are `TRUE`. Conditions separated by commas must all hold: casual riders made {n_casual_e} trips on e-bikes.

`|` means or: {n_101} trips started or ended at station 101. Equality is tested with `==`; a single `=` inside `filter()` is an error, and R's message says so.

steps.title: Order and unique rows: arrange() and distinct()

runs.task: Sort `trips` by `duration_min`, longest first, with `arrange()` and `desc()`.

runs.purpose: list each pair of start and end stations once
runs.task: List each combination of `start_station` and `end_station` once, with `distinct()`.

steps.explain:
`arrange()` sorts the rows by a column, smallest first, and `desc()` reverses that. The longest trip lasted {longest_days} days: a lost bike, found more than a week later, which is why its `end_station` is `NA`.

`distinct()` keeps one row for each combination of the columns it's given: {n_routes} pairs of start and end stations, with `NA` counted as an end.

steps.title: New columns: mutate()

runs.purpose: work out each trip's speed in km/h, as the first column
runs.task: Add a column `speed_kmh`, the distance divided by the duration in hours (`distance_km / duration_min * 60`), with `mutate()`. Put it first with `.before = 1`.

steps.explain: `mutate()` adds columns worked out from others, row by row. The first trip went {first_km} km in {first_min} minutes, so its `speed_kmh` is {first_speed}. A new column goes at the right, where a narrow Console leaves it out of the printout; `.before = 1` puts it first, where you can see it.

steps.title: Pick and arrange columns: select(), rename() and relocate()

runs.purpose: keep the trip ID, the member type and the columns about the trip's end
runs.task: Keep only `trip_id`, `member_type` and the columns whose names start with "end", with `select()` and `starts_with()`.

runs.purpose: rename `duration_min` to `minutes` and move it next to `trip_id`
runs.task: Rename `duration_min` to `minutes` with `rename()`, then move it just after `trip_id` with `relocate()`.

steps.explain:
`select()` keeps only the columns you name, in that order. `starts_with("end")` picks every column whose name starts with end: `ended_at` and `end_station`. `rename()` gives a column a new name, new name first: `minutes = duration_min`. `relocate()` moves columns without dropping any, and `.after = trip_id` puts `minutes` second.

Each `|>` hands one verb's result to the next, so a pipeline reads from top to bottom, one step per line.

steps.title: Count and summarise groups: count() and summarize()

runs.purpose: count the trips that started at each station, most first
runs.task: Count the trips for each `start_station`, the busiest first, with `count()` and `sort = TRUE`.

runs.code:
trips |>
  summarize(
    trips = n(),
    median_minutes = median(duration_min),
    .by = c(member_type, bike_type)
  )
alternatives: trips |> group_by(member_type, bike_type) |> summarize(trips = n(), median_minutes = median(duration_min), .groups = 'drop')
runs.purpose: count the trips and find their median length for each member type and bike type
runs.task: Group by `member_type` and `bike_type`. Count trips with `n()` and find median `duration_min` with `summarize()` and `.by`.

steps.explain:
`count()` counts the rows for each value of a column, and `sort = TRUE` puts the largest count first: station {top_station} was the busiest start, with {top_n} trips. `summarize()` turns each group into one row. `.by` says what makes a group, here each pair of member type and bike type, and `n()` counts the rows in it.

The median casual trip on a classic bike took {med_casual_classic} minutes; a member's on an e-bike took {med_member_electric}.

steps.title: Small groups mislead: slice_max()

runs.code:
routes <- trips |>
  summarize(
    trips = n(),
    mean_minutes = mean(duration_min),
    .by = c(start_station, end_station)
  )
alternatives: routes = trips |> summarize(trips = n(), mean_minutes = mean(duration_min), .by = c(start_station, end_station))
runs.purpose: count the trips and find their mean length for each pair of stations, in `routes`
runs.task: For each start and end station pair, count trips and find mean `duration_min`. Store the result in `routes`.

runs.purpose: sort the routes by their mean trip length, longest first
show the 5 longest routes on average, among those with at least 50 trips
runs.task: Keep the routes with at least 50 trips, then show the 5 with the highest `mean_minutes`, with `slice_max()`.

steps.explain:
`routes` has one row for each pair of stations. Sorted by their mean, the top routes have only a few trips each: the first has {top_trips} and a mean of {top_mean} minutes, because one lost bike pulls a small group's mean a long way.

(An `NA` end station groups the trips no dock recorded the end of.) Leaving out the `NA` ends wouldn't fix this: among the routes that end at a station, the five with the longest mean have at most {real_top_trips} trips each.

Among the routes with at least 50 trips, `slice_max()` shows the 5 with the longest mean, the first at {big_top_mean} minutes, a believable ride. Before trusting a group's average, check how many rows it has.
